articles.title: Should My Five-Year-Old Already Be Reading?
articles.standfirst: Reading readiness begins long before a child decodes their first sentence. Here is what to notice, and what genuinely matters at this age.

image.alt: A parent and child sharing a picture book

articles.title: My Child Hates Writing. What Do I Do?
articles.standfirst: The bottleneck is almost never imagination. Separating the thinking from the handwriting lets both of them get easier.

image.alt: A child pausing over an open exercise book

articles.title: Math Anxiety: Why Kids Struggle (and What Helps)
articles.standfirst: Math confidence grows from curiosity and hands-on experiences, not pressure.

image.alt: A child working with counting blocks at a table

articles.title: How Much Homework Is Too Much?
articles.standfirst: There is a point where the evening costs more than the worksheet returns. The research is clearer about where that point sits than schools tend to be.

image.alt: A parent sitting beside a child at a homework table

articles.title: My Toddler Won't Sit Still to Learn Anything
articles.standfirst: At three, sitting still is not the state learning happens in. Almost everything a child of this age takes in arrives through movement.

image.alt: A toddler moving between play materials on the floor

articles.title: Why Doesn't My Child Listen the First Time?
articles.standfirst: Selective hearing is rarely selective. Working memory offers a plainer explanation, and a fix that does not involve raising your voice.

image.alt: A parent crouching to speak with a child at eye level

articles.title: Big Feelings, Little Bodies: Understanding Tantrums
articles.standfirst: Tantrums are communication, not manipulation. Let's understand what's really going on.

image.alt: A young child mid-tantrum with a parent close by

articles.title: Should I Punish or Explain?
articles.standfirst: A consequence a child cannot connect to the act is just a punishment with better branding. The connection is the whole mechanism.

image.alt: A parent and child talking together on a doorstep

articles.title: My Teenager Has Stopped Talking to Me
articles.standfirst: The silence is developmental before it is personal. What reopens the conversation is usually sideways, not direct.

image.alt: A parent and teenager walking side by side

articles.title: My Child Keeps Falling Out With Friends. Should I Step In?
articles.standfirst: Conflict isn't always something adults need to remove. Here's how to support without taking over.

image.alt: Two children sorting something out in a playground

articles.title: My Child Doesn't Want to Share
articles.standfirst: Before about four, sharing on demand asks for something the brain has not built yet. There is a better thing to teach in the meantime.

image.alt: Two young children playing with the same set of blocks

articles.title: Is My Child Being Left Out or Just Quiet?
articles.standfirst: Slow to warm is a temperament, not a deficit. The pressure to fix it is usually what does the damage.

image.alt: A child watching a group before joining in

articles.title: How Do I Talk to My Child About Bullying?
articles.standfirst: The conversation that works is the one had before anything happens, and it sounds nothing like a warning.

image.alt: A parent and child sitting together on a sofa talking

articles.title: How Do I Build Confidence Without Empty Praise?
articles.standfirst: Some encouragement makes a child more fragile, not less. The difference sits in one word, and most of us reach for the wrong one.

image.alt: A parent watching a child finish something on their own

articles.title: My Child Gives Up Before Trying. Why?
articles.standfirst: Quitting early is often a prediction rather than a preference. Changing the prediction takes smaller wins than you would expect.

image.alt: A child part way through a difficult build

articles.title: Is My Teenager's Self Doubt Normal?
articles.standfirst: Around thirteen, self image gets rebuilt from the outside in. Knowing that is happening makes it easier not to argue with it.

image.alt: A teenager at a window in thought

articles.title: How Much Sleep Does My Child Actually Need?
articles.standfirst: Consolidation, mood and attention all run on the same overnight process. An hour of lost sleep shows up in all three by Thursday.

image.alt: A child settled in bed with a bedside lamp on

articles.title: My Child Is a Fussy Eater. Should I Worry?
articles.standfirst: Most narrow eating between two and six is a developmental stage with a predictable exit. A few signs are worth acting on.

image.alt: A family meal with a child considering the food

articles.title: How Do I Know If My Child Is Anxious?
articles.standfirst: Anxiety at this age rarely announces itself. It arrives as stomach aches, stalling and anger, which is why it gets missed.

image.alt: A parent sitting close to a child at the end of the day

articles.title: When Should I Start Teaching Body Safety?
articles.standfirst: Earlier than most families expect, and in plainer words. The vocabulary matters more than the conversation.

image.alt: A parent and young child talking at bath time

articles.title: How Do I Talk About Strangers Without Scaring My Child?
articles.standfirst: The stranger rule is the least useful part of keeping a child safe. What replaces it is more specific and less frightening.

image.alt: A parent and child walking together in a busy street

articles.title: Is My Teenager Safe Online?
articles.standfirst: Monitoring buys less than most parents hope. What actually protects a teenager is whether they will tell you when something goes wrong.

image.alt: A teenager and parent talking at a kitchen table

articles.title: How Much Screen Time Is Too Much?
articles.standfirst: Two hours of one thing and two hours of another do completely different work on a child. Counting minutes hides the difference.

image.alt: A family evening with a device set aside on the table

articles.title: Raising Children in a Digital World
articles.standfirst: Tools are here to stay. Our role is to help children use them wisely and mindfully.

image.alt: A child using a tablet at a table at home

articles.title: Should My Child Be Using AI for Homework?
articles.standfirst: The question is not whether they use it. It is which part of the thinking gets skipped, and whether that part mattered.

image.alt: A teenager working at a desk with notes and a laptop

articles.title: When Should My Child Get a Phone?
articles.standfirst: The talk that matters happens about two years before the phone arrives, and it is not about rules.

image.alt: A parent and child talking on a sofa

articles.title: Why Does Turning Off the Screen Cause a Meltdown?
articles.standfirst: The transition, not the screen, is what your child is reacting to. Which puts the fix before the switch rather than after it.

image.alt: A child being given a warning before a screen goes off

articles.title: When Should Children Learn About Money?
articles.standfirst: Money habits are largely set by about seven. What builds them is smaller and more ordinary than a lesson.

image.alt: A child counting coins at a table with a parent

articles.title: Should I Give My Child Pocket Money?
articles.standfirst: Tied to chores or given freely changes what the money teaches. Both work, but not for the same thing.

image.alt: A child putting money into a savings tin

articles.title: What Should a Fourteen-Year-Old Be Able to Do Alone?
articles.standfirst: Judgement is built by making decisions that carry weight. Most teenagers are handed neither the weight nor the decision.

image.alt: A teenager cooking a meal in a home kitchen

articles.title: How Do I Teach Respect Without Teaching Fear?
articles.standfirst: Many of us were raised on obedience and want something different. The tradition has more to offer than the version we inherited.

image.alt: Three generations of a family together at home

articles.title: My Child Is Losing Our Mother Tongue
articles.standfirst: A common worry and a solvable one. What keeps a language alive at home is far smaller than a curriculum.

image.alt: A grandparent reading aloud to a child

articles.title: How Do I Pass on Our Values Without Lecturing?
articles.standfirst: Children absorb what a household repeats, not what it announces. The distinction decides whether any of it survives adolescence.

image.alt: A family preparing food together in a kitchen

articles.title: Why Do I Feel Guilty at Nine Every Night?
articles.standfirst: Almost every parent replays the day once the house goes quiet. Here is what that replay is for, and when it stops being useful.

image.alt: A parent sitting alone in a quiet living room in the evening

articles.title: We Are Both Exhausted. How Do We Do This?
articles.standfirst: Two tired adults negotiating an evening is its own problem, separate from the children, and it deserves its own plan.

image.alt: Two parents talking at the end of the day

articles.title: Am I Comparing My Child Too Much?
articles.standfirst: Another parent mentions what their child is already doing and the evening curdles. A short note on where that feeling comes from.

image.alt: Parents talking at a school gate
